speaker: Karri Saarinen
title: Inside Linear: Building with taste, craft, and focus | Karri Saarinen
question: Why does product-market fit behave differently in B2B software than in consumer social apps?
guest: Thinking of product-market fit as a spectrum is a good way to frame it. There's this idea from older blog posts that you just know when you have product-market fit, and that's probably true for some consumer social apps where you don't really have lots of different segments—you just have millions of users, you see it taking off, and you have fit. In B2B, you always have different sizes of customers, different domains, and different categories, so you might be doing really well in one category and not well in another. The counterintuitive thing is that when you're doing really well in one category, you should double down on it. Eric from Zoom told me the same thing—when universities worked well for them early on, they asked how to get more universities rather than trying to go after everyone at once, which isn't possible. If you see something working really well, focus on doing more of that until you have that category captured, and only then expand to a new area.

points.core: Consumer social apps experience relatively uniform demand where takeoff feels binary.
points.note: Accept: consumer social products serve a broad homogeneous user base where viral growth makes PMF immediately obvious. Do not credit: generic statements that consumer apps grow faster.

points.core: B2B markets fracture across company sizes, making product-market fit strictly segment-specific.
points.note: Accept: B2B customers differ sharply by size, industry, or category, so a product can have strong fit in one segment and weak fit in another. Do not credit: generic mentions of longer B2B sales cycles or procurement.

points.core: Winning one narrow B2B segment requires doubling down until captured before expanding outward.
points.note: Accept: concentrating on a single category showing strong pull (like startups or universities) rather than chasing every customer type at once. Do not credit: generic advice to 'focus on a niche' without the sequential capture-then-expand dynamic.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Product-market fit differs because the two markets differ in who buys, why they buy, and how value is created.

In B2B software, the buyer is often not the user, and purchases are deliberate: a company pays to solve a defined problem with measurable ROI. Fit therefore shows up early and legibly, through willingness to pay, shortening sales cycles, renewals, and expansion revenue. You can find it with a handful of customers, validate it through conversations, and it tends to be durable, since switching costs, integrations, and contracts lock it in. The risk is false fit: a few bespoke deals that don't generalize.

In consumer social apps, the product is free, the value comes from other users, and the need is emotional rather than economic. Fit can't be validated by asking people or by revenue; it appears only in behavior, namely retention curves, engagement frequency, and organic growth. Because value depends on network density, the product may feel worthless until it reaches critical mass, then take off suddenly. Fit is also more fragile, as tastes shift and switching costs are low, so it is more binary, harder to predict, and easier to lose.

points.why: The response attributes binary takeoff to network density and critical mass without establishing relatively uniform demand across consumer social users.
The warning about bespoke deals does not explain how differences in company size, industry, or category can produce strong fit in one B2B segment and weak fit in another.
The response offers no strategy to double down on a B2B segment showing strong pull, capture it, and then expand.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Product-market fit behaves differently because B2B software is governed by rational economic value and switching costs, whereas consumer social apps depend on network density and social psychology. In B2B, organizations pay to solve explicit operational problems like cutting costs, saving time, or reducing risk, often tolerating clunky interfaces when the return is clear. Because buyers are frequently separate from end users and adoption embeds software into core workflows and data, B2B fit builds incrementally, sticks durably, and compounds through renewals and account expansion.

Consumer social apps, by contrast, offer almost no standalone utility; value emerges only when a critical mass of peers or creators participates simultaneously. Fit is therefore threshold-driven rather than gradual, fueled by emotional rewards like status, entertainment, and belonging long before monetization begins. Where B2B fit is proven by willingness to pay, consumer social fit shows up in viral growth and habitual daily retention, yet remains fragile because fading novelty or shifting cultural norms can trigger rapid network unraveling.

points.why: The response explains abrupt takeoff through network critical mass and leaves out relatively uniform demand across consumer users.
The response explains how B2B fit deepens within accounts and leaves out how fit varies across company sizes, industries, or categories.
The response mentions account expansion and omits the strategy of concentrating on a segment with strong demand until it is captured before entering another segment.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Product-market fit works differently because the buyer, the value, and the reasons people keep using the product are all different.

In B2B software, value is mostly functional and can be measured. The product saves time, makes money, or reduces risk for a specific workflow, so fit shows up in clear signals: customers renew, accounts grow over time (net revenue retention), sales cycles get shorter, and buyers will pay before the product is polished. Fit is usually reached one segment at a time. A few dozen customers paying a lot each can prove it, and contracts, integrations, and switching costs keep them from leaving.

Consumer social apps get their value from network effects. The product is only worth using if your friends are on it, so fit depends on how many users there are and how densely they're connected, not on solving a task. Early signs can mislead, because novelty can drive a big spike in downloads that then collapses. The real test is retention curves that level off and daily-to-monthly engagement ratios. Users pay nothing and can leave in seconds, so fit is fragile. It comes from habit and network density rather than contracts, and it can disappear quickly when the culture moves on.

points.why: The response emphasizes network density and potentially misleading growth spikes, leaving out the link between relatively uniform demand and unmistakable takeoff.
The response says fit is reached one segment at a time but omits how differences across customer groups cause fit to vary by segment.
The response gives no strategy for doubling down on a segment with strong demand until it is captured and then expanding.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer: Product-market fit behaves differently in B2B software than in consumer social apps because of who decides to adopt the product, how value is created, and how sticky that value becomes. In B2B software, the buyer is often separate from the end user, and adoption depends on measurable ROI, workflow integration, security, and budget approval. Because a B2B tool can deliver immediate standalone utility to one organization, fit usually emerges gradually within a narrow niche and shows up through low churn, net revenue retention, and repeatable sales. Once embedded in company workflows, high switching costs make that fit durable. Consumer social apps, by contrast, depend on individual impulse, emotion, and habit, with almost no friction to try or abandon. Their value comes primarily from network effects rather than standalone utility, so fit is far more binary and volatile: growth can explode through viral loops once a critical mass forms, yet disappear just as quickly when cultural trends or user attention shift elsewhere.

points.why: The response attributes binary takeoff to network effects and critical mass without connecting it to relatively uniform demand across a broad user base.
The response says fit emerges within a narrow niche but never explains how differences in company size, industry, or category can produce strong fit in one segment and weak fit in another.
The response does not say to double down on a segment showing strong demand and capture it before expanding.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
In B2B software, product-market fit comes from solving a recurring business problem well enough that companies will pay for the solution, adopt it, and renew. The buyer and the daily user are often different people, so the product has to deliver value to both. Fit can start in a narrow segment, and sales cycles can make it slow to confirm even when customers who adopt the product get clear value.

In consumer social apps, much of the value comes from who else is there and what they do. People may love the idea and still leave if their friends are absent or their feed is quiet. Fit can emerge quickly once enough of the right people join and interact, and it can fade when that activity drops. Repeat engagement within a community tells you more than a spike in downloads.

points.why: The response describes how network effects can drive rapid uptake within a community but does not link broad, relatively uniform demand to an obvious takeoff.
The response says fit can start in a narrow segment but does not explain how differences among B2B customers can produce strong fit in one segment and weak fit in another.
The response mentions starting in a narrow segment but does not call for doubling down on a segment with strong demand until it is captured before expanding.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
In B2B software, product-market fit often means a specific type of company gets enough value from solving a recurring problem to keep paying. The buyer and the daily user may be different people, so adoption and renewal tell you different things. A sales team can win an initial contract, and switching costs can keep it in place. Repeated use, measurable results, and similar customers renewing or expanding give you stronger evidence of fit.

In consumer social apps, users can usually try the product for free and leave just as easily. Its value often depends on who else shows up and what they contribute. The same app can feel indispensable in one school and empty in the next. That makes return visits, interaction, and invitations within a community more revealing than download totals. A B2B company can often validate fit one customer at a time. A social app may need a whole group to adopt before any one person has a reason to stay.

points.why: The response emphasizes that social app value varies by community and omits the broad, relatively uniform demand that makes takeoff immediately apparent.
The response describes evidence of fit among similar companies but does not explain how differences between B2B segments can produce strong fit in one and weak fit in another.
The response discusses validating fit customer by customer and omits the strategy of concentrating on a promising segment until it is captured before expanding.
